title: Coffee: Attempt #1
text: You pour a coffee into the CRUSH IT mug from a 2018 sales offsite. You lift it. From the floor: "{ME}. Hold my hand. No. The coffee hand."

choices.label: Switch hands. Become ambidextrous.

outcomes.text: You move the mug to your left hand. They grab your left hand. You switch back. They switch with you. On lap five you drain it in one gulp. Hand: available.
Four laps of hand-switching. By lap five the coffee is lukewarm, {kid} wins, and it all goes on the rug. The mug lands upright, unharmed, still saying CRUSH IT. The mug always survives.

choices.label: "One second, sweetheart." Set it down.

outcomes.text: One second becomes eleven minutes and four books. The coffee is cold when you get back, with a single puff floating in the middle. You drink around it.
One second becomes eleven minutes. {kid} has made you a fresh one: the cold coffee, plus a raisin, plus a toy block. They're watching. You sip. "Mmm." You've never loved anyone more or a drink less.

choices.label: Drink it scalding. Like it owes you money.

outcomes.text: You drink it at the temperature of a car hood in July. You can no longer taste. You can, however, hear colors.
Too hot. You burn the roof of your mouth and make a face {kid} learns instantly. By lunch they're doing it at daycare. They call it "the coffee face."

title: Coffee: Reheat #4
text: The CRUSH IT mug has been microwaved four times since 7 AM and drunk zero times. It has a skin now. The microwave beeps. It beeps again. It is beeping at you, specifically.

choices.label: Reheat #5. Stand guard this time.

outcomes.text: You stand at the microwave for the full 90 seconds, arms crossed, daring it. Beep. You drink it hot, in front of a witness. The witness asks for some.
At 0:04, from the living room: "{ME}! COME SEE!" You go see. It's a crumb. A good crumb, to be fair. Reheat #6 is scheduled for later.

choices.label: Drink it cold. Call it cold brew.

outcomes.text: Cold brew is $6.50 at the place with the reclaimed-wood counter. Yours has a skin and was free. You're basically making money.

choices.label: Fresh pot. Start over as a new person.

outcomes.text: Eight minutes of brewing. In that time {kid} takes every magnet off the fridge and lines them up on the floor, by size. You drink a hot, fresh coffee and admire the exhibit.
While the pot gurgles, {kid} takes the old mug and waters the fern with it. The fern looks more alert than it has in years. Twenty minutes later, so do you.

choices.label: Tea party. Serve it in the tiny cups.

outcomes.text: {kid} serves your cold coffee back to you in a teacup the size of a thimble, eleven times, in eleven accents. "Your grown-up soup." You get about a tablespoon in total. Five stars.
The party ends when the guest of honor, a stuffed giraffe, is accused of drinking it all. The giraffe goes in time-out. You're still thirsty, but justice was done.

title: Coffee: Have You Seen This Mug?
text: The CRUSH IT mug was in your hand four minutes ago. Full. Hot. Now it's not anywhere. You've checked the fridge. You've checked your other hand. {kid} is humming.

choices.label: Search the house. Every room. Twice.

outcomes.text: You find three socks, the remote, a crayon in the butter and a shoelace tied, tightly, to a chair. No mug. The house gives you everything except what you asked for.
Two full sweeps, and all you find is the mug's coaster. Just the coaster, on the bathroom floor, with nothing on it. Somehow that's worse.

choices.label: Interrogate the witness.

outcomes.text: "Where's my coffee?" "It's sleeping." "Where?" "In its house." "Where's its house?" A finger goes to their lips. The witness has been advised not to answer.
{kid} leads you, very seriously, to the toy kitchen and hands you an empty plastic cup. "Careful. Hot." You blow on it. You fake a long sip. They refill it. Best café in town. No coffee.

choices.label: Make another. Let the first one go.

outcomes.text: You make a second coffee in the backup mug, the free one from the dentist. It works fine. It just doesn't believe in you the way CRUSH IT did.

title: Coffee: The Point of No Return
text: It's after 3. You have about forty minutes of person left and four hours of day. A coffee now gets you to bedtime. It also gets you to 1:30 AM, awake, re-planning the kitchen.

choices.label: Double espresso. Tonight is a rumor.

outcomes.text: It hits in six minutes. By minute twelve you've emptied the dishwasher, reloaded it correctly and given the junk drawer a theme. The theme is "batteries?"
It works too well. You start talking at 1.5x speed, and by dinner {kid} is talking at 1.5x back. You're both narrating the same snack, faster and faster.

choices.label: Half-caf. A coward's compromise.

outcomes.text: Half the caffeine. Half the guilt. All of the 1:30 AM. Your body doesn't do fractions.

choices.label: Lie face-down on the rug. Four minutes.

outcomes.text: {kid} uses you as a rug, then a horse, then a bed, then a rug again. It isn't caffeine. But it's horizontal.
Ninety seconds in, {kid} sits on your back and announces, "I'm the boss of you." You don't argue. You can't. They're sitting on your lungs.

choices.label: Just smell the coffee bag. Deeply.

outcomes.text: You put your face in the bag of beans and inhale. It does nothing. It does something. It does nothing.

title: Coffee: Cold Case
text: You open the microwave to heat a pouch. Inside, in the dark: the CRUSH IT mug, full, cold, missing for days. {kid} can't reach the microwave. There is only one suspect.

choices.label: Reheat it. One last time. For closure.

outcomes.text: Ninety seconds. You drink it. It tastes like a version of you who still had plans for this coffee. It's not bad, which is the worst part.
Thirty seconds in, the microwave starts sparking. CRUSH IT has a gold rim. It was a nice offsite. You yank the plug. The mug is fine. The mug is always fine.

choices.label: Hold a small funeral. {kid} officiates.

outcomes.text: {kid} says a few words: "Bye, coffee. You was hot." You pour it on the flower bed together, and {kid} pats the dirt. It's the most moving service you've been to in years.

choices.label: Pour it out. Fresh cup. Tell no one.

outcomes.text: Down the sink. Fresh cup. You stick a note on the microwave: "CHECK FOR COFFEE." By tomorrow you'll have stopped seeing the note. That's how it starts.
Rinsed, refilled, back in service: CRUSH IT, hot again. You lift it. From the floor: "{ME}. Hold my hand. The coffee hand." It's Monday again, spiritually.

title: Tantrum #1: Garbage Day
text: The garbage truck came, took the garbage and left without honking. {kid} is face-down on the front step. You start a tally on the fridge. You leave room.

choices.label: Chase the truck. Both of you. Go.

outcomes.text: A block and a half in slippers, {kid} on your hip, both of you waving. The driver sees. The driver honks twice. {kid} will bring this up at their wedding.
The truck turns the corner as you reach the hydrant. You're on a public sidewalk in slippers, holding a sobbing child, waving at nothing. A neighbor waves back, unsure.

choices.label: "It comes back next Tuesday."

outcomes.text: "Next Tuesday" means very little to someone who has only had 104 Tuesdays. The protest holds the step for nine minutes. Then a bird lands. Truck who?
They accept it. Then they ask if it's next Tuesday. Then again, every twenty minutes, until bedtime. It is not next Tuesday. It is never next Tuesday.

choices.label: Be the truck. Wheel the bin out, beeping.

outcomes.text: You wheel the bin to the curb doing the reverse beep. {kid} stops crying to supervise. You beep the whole way back. You'll be beeping on request until spring.
You beep the bin to the curb. Across the street, a retired neighbor starts beeping too, unprompted. Now there are two trucks. {kid} is delighted and slightly afraid.

choices.label: Garbage truck videos. One. Okay, four.

outcomes.text: Fifteen minutes of garbage trucks from around the world. {kid} is calm and has a new favorite truck, which is Belgian. The screen-off is going to be a whole thing.

title: Tantrum #2: Put It Back
text: Tally: 2. A leaf has fallen off the tree in the front yard, and {kid} saw it happen. They want it put back. Not near the tree. ON the tree. They're watching your hands.

choices.label: Tape it back on. Packing tape. Commit.

outcomes.text: You tape the leaf to the branch while a neighbor walks a dog past. Slowly. Twice. {kid} inspects the repair and approves it. In a month you'll have to explain autumn.
You tape it on. Another leaf falls. Then two more. The tree is fighting back. {kid} looks at you like a contractor who blew the deadline.

choices.label: Explain the seasons. All four.

outcomes.text: You cover autumn, chlorophyll and the life cycle of deciduous trees. {kid} listens to all of it, then says, "Put it BACK." You were never in a conversation.
Halfway through photosynthesis, the crying stops so they can ask what photosynthesis is. Then why. Then why. You've traded a tantrum for a seminar.

choices.label: Hand them an identical leaf. Say nothing.

outcomes.text: You present a matching leaf with total confidence. They accept it, put it in their pocket and say, "Now the other one." There is always another one.
{kid} holds it up to the light like a jeweler, then hands it back. "This one is from the GROUND." The crying resumes at a higher altitude.

title: Tantrum #3: Hurricane Agnes
text: The fridge tally says 3. You've started naming them alphabetically, like the weather service. Hurricane Agnes has formed over the moon being out in the daytime, which nobody cleared with {kid}.

choices.label: Yell "GO HOME, MOON" together.

outcomes.text: You stand in the driveway and yell at the moon. {kid} joins in. The moon stays put. But you're on the same side now, which was the whole trick.
You yell at the moon. The neighbor's kid comes out and yells at the moon. Then the neighbor. Agnes breaks up into a block party.

choices.label: Close the blinds on the moon.

outcomes.text: Blinds down. Moon gone. {kid} declares victory over the moon and is extremely nice to you for an hour, the way generals are after a war.
Blinds down. Agnes weakens to a tropical sulk. Then {kid} opens one slat, sees the moon and re-forms at full strength.

choices.label: Sunshine Sing-Along. Corduroy man has this.

outcomes.text: The man in corduroy sings a song about the moon, by coincidence or witchcraft. Agnes is downgraded at once. The screen-off forecast is not good.

title: Tantrum #4: Hurricane Bernard
text: You've started live-texting the tantrums to {partner}, the way storm chasers do.

messages.text: cause: i said yes too fast
a banana. they wanted to ask twice

choices.label: "Cat 4. Bring plywood and crackers."

outcomes.text: Twenty-five minutes later {partner} walks in with crackers and the face of a first responder. Bernard is a light drizzle by then. They take full credit.
You laugh at the "lol." Bernard sees you laughing at your phone and upgrades to a Category 5.

choices.label: Phone down. Lie on the floor with them.

outcomes.text: You lie on the kitchen tile next to Bernard. Bernard hiccups twice, then puts their head on your arm. Storm over. You never send the all-clear.

choices.label: Send a video. Narrate it like the news.

outcomes.text: "Bernard is moving slowly west, toward the snack drawer." {partner} watches it in a meeting with the sound on. Four coworkers are now following the storm.
You can't tell if it's support or a bit. It's both. With them it's always both.

title: Tantrum #5: Hurricane Clara
text: The library elevator. A man in a fleece vest has just pressed the button. {kid}'s button. The man doesn't know yet. {kid} is drawing the longest breath of their career.

choices.label: "Sir, could you un-press it?"

outcomes.text: The man looks at you, then at {kid}, and understands everything. A slow, solemn mime of un-pressing. A small bow. {kid} presses it. Clara dissipates. You'd follow this man into battle.
"Un-press it?" the man repeats, loudly, for the whole lobby. Clara makes landfall between the large-print books and a man doing taxes.

choices.label: Press every button. All of them.

outcomes.text: You lift {kid} to the panel. They press 1 through 6. The elevator stops at every floor. The man in the fleece vest rides along in silence, gets off at 6 and waits for the next one.
They press 1 through 6, then the red one. The alarm is very loud and very brief. The librarian has a face for this. It has been used before.

choices.label: "STAIRS! Who wants the STAIRS?"

outcomes.text: Forty-two stairs, every one counted out loud. Clara blows out to sea around 19. By the top, you're the one who needs the elevator.

choices.label: Freeze

outcomes.text: "THAT MAN TOOKED MY BUTTON." The lobby turns around. The man says "Sorry, buddy," and is now, forever, the man who tooked the button.

title: Tantrum #6: Disaster Relief
text: Tally: 6. Hurricane Desmond. The cause: {kid}'s shadow won't stop following them, and you are "not doing ANYTHING about it." You open the disaster relief website, one-handed.

choices.label: File the claim. Cause of disaster: "shadow."

outcomes.text: Claim #44718 submitted. Expected response: 6 to 8 weeks. Desmond blows itself out in four minutes, which you add to the claim as a note.
The form asks, "Is this an emergency?" You look at the floor. You click yes. Desmond, sensing paperwork, intensifies.

choices.label: Make the shadow a friend. Flashlight. Puppets.

outcomes.text: Blinds down, flashlight on. The shadow becomes a dog, a bird, a very bad crab. By minute twenty the shadow is named Doug and has been invited to dinner.
Flashlight on. The shadow is now nine feet tall, on the wall, right behind them. {kid} turns around slowly. You've made the problem bigger. Literally.

choices.label: Stomp on the shadow. Show it who's boss.

outcomes.text: You stomp the shadow. It moves. You stomp again. {kid} stops crying to watch an adult lose a fight to the sun.
You stomp. They stomp. Soon you're both stomping the driveway, red-faced, yelling at a shadow. It doesn't help with the shadow. It helps with everything else.

choices.label: Tablet. Accept the relief package.

outcomes.text: Relief arrives as a man in corduroy. The shadow is forgotten. You've accepted federal aid, and federal aid comes with strings.

title: Tantrum #7: Hurricane {me}
text: You step on a wooden block and say "NNNGH" for nine full seconds. {kid} pats your arm. "Big feelings, {me}? Smell the flower. Blow the candle." Then they go to the fridge and add a tally. Under your name.

choices.label: Smell the flower. Blow the candle.

outcomes.text: You smell the flower. You blow the candle. They watch, nodding, like the world's smallest yoga teacher. It works, which is humiliating. They give you a sticker.
You blow the candle too hard. "Gentle, {me}." You do it again, gently. They make you do it four more times, for practice. You've never been so calm or so supervised.

choices.label: "I am NOT having a tantrum."

outcomes.text: "You're having a tantrum," they say, gently. Your voice goes up an octave explaining that you're not. They walk back to the fridge and add a second tally.
"Okay," they say, kindly, in your exact voice, with your exact head tilt. It's what you say to them. It's unbearable to hear.

choices.label: Lie on the floor and kick. Show them how.

outcomes.text: You lie on the floor and kick. {kid} watches with professional interest, then lies down next to you and does it better. {partner} walks in, assesses the scene and lies down too.
You lie on the floor and kick. {kid} studies your form and gives notes: "More legs." You do more legs. It feels incredible. Nobody tells you this part.

title: Food #1: Ruled Spicy
text: Plain pasta. No sauce, no salt, nothing. {kid} takes one bite and pushes the bowl away. "It's spicy." It is not spicy. It has never been spicy. That's their testimony, and they're sticking to it.

choices.label: Take a bite. Testify: not spicy.

outcomes.text: You eat a forkful. "Mmm. Not spicy." {kid} watches you swallow, then rules: "Spicy for you too." The court has expanded its ruling.
"See? Not spicy." {kid} takes a cautious bite, chews for a long time and announces, "You fixed it." You did nothing. Nobody needs to know.

choices.label: Agree. "Whoa. SO spicy." Fan your mouth.

outcomes.text: You gasp and fan your mouth. {kid} is thrilled. They eat the whole bowl, gasping between bites, the bravest person who ever lived.
"SO spicy," you gasp. {kid} nods, vindicated, and pushes the bowl even further away. You've just entered their testimony into the record.

choices.label: "Then you're done." Clear the plate.

outcomes.text: You clear it without a word. Forty minutes later: "I'm HUNGRY. I want the pasta." The pasta has been ruled delicious, retroactively, from the bin.

title: Food #2: False Advertising
text: {kid} is holding a chicken nugget up next to the bag. The nugget on the bag has a smile and a little chef's hat. This one has neither. They allege false advertising. Honestly, they have a case.

choices.label: Ketchup face. Napkin hat. Full restoration.

outcomes.text: Two dots, a smile and a tiny napkin hat. The nugget is now a client. {kid} talks to it for six minutes, apologizes and eats it head first.
You draw the face. {kid} stares at it for a long time. "Now he's sad, because I'm eating him." Lunch is cancelled out of respect.

choices.label: Point to the fine print: "Serving suggestion."

outcomes.text: You point at the tiny words under the picture. {kid} can't read. {kid} can tell when they're being lawyered. The nuggets are thrown, one at a time, as damages.
"Serving suggestion," you read. {kid} considers this, then suggests serving them to you. You eat four nuggets over the sink. It's the first lunch you've had this week.

choices.label: Help them write the nugget company a complaint.

outcomes.text: {kid} dictates: "Dear nugget. You lied. Love, {kid}." You fold it into an envelope and mail it to nobody, and they eat four nuggets while waiting for a reply.

choices.label: Settle out of court. One cracker.

outcomes.text: A cracker, no admission of wrongdoing. {kid} accepts the settlement and eats it. The nuggets go in the bin. Their lawyer will open with crackers next time.

title: Food #3: The Beige Doctrine
text: {kid} now eats only beige food: pasta, crackers and one specific bread. You slipped a piece of cauliflower onto the plate. It is also beige. It was identified and expelled in under a second.

choices.label: Argue it's beige. Hold it next to a cracker.

outcomes.text: You hold the cauliflower next to a cracker under the kitchen light. A perfect match. {kid} studies them both, then points at the cauliflower: "That one's lying."
"Beige," you say, holding it next to a cracker. {kid} squints, shrugs and eats it. Then another. You've found a loophole. Never mention it again, or it closes.

choices.label: Accept the doctrine. Serve beige until spring.

outcomes.text: Toast, rice, noodles, a pale apple slice. Everything gets eaten. The daycare form asks about "variety in the diet." You write "tan."

choices.label: Hide it in a pancake. Beige on beige.

outcomes.text: You blend the cauliflower into pancake batter. It's beige. It's a pancake. They eat three, then look at you with a quiet suspicion they'll carry into adulthood.
They eat the whole pancake around one tiny, intact piece of cauliflower, which they set on the edge of the plate like a hair they found in soup.

title: Food #4: I'm a Dog Now
text: {kid} has become a dog. Dogs, they explain, eat off the floor, don't use forks and are not subject to the vegetable laws. The dog would like its food in a bowl, on the floor, now. The dog knows its rights.

choices.label: Serve the dog. Bowl, floor, clean mat.

outcomes.text: The dog eats everything, carrots included, face-first. It's the best they've eaten all week, and it was served on the floor. Draw your own conclusions.
The dog eats three bites, barks at a leaf, then asks for "dog water" in a cup. A cup. With a straw. Dogs aren't consistent either.

choices.label: Become a dog too. Eat beside them.

outcomes.text: You get on all fours and eat cold noodles from a bowl next to theirs. The dog finishes everything just to keep up. Through the window, the mail carrier makes eye contact and decides not to knock.

choices.label: "Good dogs sit at the table."

outcomes.text: Accepted. Good dogs sit at the table and use a fork. Good dogs, it turns out, also get a treat, and this dog knows exactly which cabinet.
"I'm a BAD dog," they inform you, and eat their noodles off the floor with their whole face, holding your gaze.

title: Food #5: The Returns Desk
text: {kid} isn't refusing their peas. They're returning them. One at a time, overhand, off the high chair, with eye contact and a small, polite "No thank you" for each pea.

choices.label: "Food stays on the table." (Say it 40 times.)

outcomes.text: You say it calmly. A pea leaves the tray. You say it again. The next pea leaves more slowly, so they can watch your face. This is no longer about peas.
You say it once. They hold the next pea over the edge for a long time, looking at you. Then they eat it. You don't move. You don't breathe. They eat nine.

choices.label: Open a returns desk: a "no thank you" bowl.

outcomes.text: A small bowl where unwanted food can go, politely. It works. Peas go in the bowl, not on the floor. {kid} even eats two, out of professional courtesy.
They love the no-thank-you bowl. Every pea goes in it. Then the bowl goes on the floor, politely. "No thank you, bowl."

choices.label: Accept all returns. Mop in March.

outcomes.text: Pea after pea, each with a "No thank you." Around pea 40 you stop hearing the thank-yous. The last pea will surface in July, in the dryer.

title: Food #6: Yesterday Food
text: Leftovers: the pasta {kid} begged for yesterday, by name, eleven times. Today it's been ruled "yesterday food." They'll only eat what you're eating, off your plate. You're eating the same pasta.

choices.label: Swap plates. Same pasta, new jurisdiction.

outcomes.text: You swap. They eat everything on your former plate. You eat everything on theirs. They watch you finish, then say, quietly, "That was mine."
You swap. They want to swap back. You swap back. Seven swaps. The pasta is cold and nobody has eaten, but everyone has been extremely fair.

choices.label: Share one plate. A bite each.

outcomes.text: Bite for bite, off one plate. They count your bites out loud and eat exactly as many. It's the most they've eaten in days. You got half a meal, a personal best.

choices.label: "You get what you get."

outcomes.text: "You get what you get and you don't get upset," you say. They repeat it back, word for word, and get upset. Then they eat a roll, out of spite.
They get what they get. They don't get upset. They eat it, every noodle, while you stand there with your mouth open, which is when they put a noodle in it.

choices.label: Cereal. Concede the case.

outcomes.text: Cereal, poured with the dignity of a lawyer leaving through the courthouse back door. Two bowls. The pasta goes back in the fridge, to be refused again tomorrow.

title: Snack #1: The Wrapper
text: You open a granola bar in the pantry with the door shut, peeling the wrapper one millimeter at a time. From two rooms away: "WHAT'S THAT NOISE."

choices.label: "It's spicy." (It's oats.)

outcomes.text: "It's spicy," you call, chewing. A long pause. "Okay." Footsteps go back to the blocks. You've learned their language. Use it sparingly. They're listening.
"It's spicy." A pause. Then footsteps, coming closer. "I LIKE spicy now." A small hand appears. You've been out-lawyered by someone who can't open the pantry.

choices.label: Split it. Half each. (Mostly theirs.)

outcomes.text: You break it in half. They take the bigger half, then the smaller half, then lick the wrapper. You eat a crumb off your own shirt. Lunch.

choices.label: Eat it in one bite. Destroy the evidence.

outcomes.text: Gone in one bite. They arrive to an empty pantry and a parent humming with their mouth closed. "What was that noise?" "Mm?" You'll take it to your grave.
You get the whole bar in. They arrive. You smile with your mouth shut. They study your cheeks, then leave without a word. Days later, Ms. Patty asks, very gently, what a "mouth bar" is.

title: Snack #2: Name That Snack
text: "I want the crunchy ones from the time." Which crunchy ones. Which time. {kid}'s bottom lip has started to go. You have about six seconds.

choices.label: "The fish crackers!"

outcomes.text: Correct! You hand them over with a game-show flourish. They eat them like a contestant who knew the answer all along.
"NOT FISH." The lip goes all the way. They eat the fish crackers anyway, sobbing, on principle.

choices.label: "The puffs from the car!"

outcomes.text: "YES." They're in the car. The car is in the driveway. You both go out in socks, in the drizzle, for puffs. Worth it.
"NO. From the OTHER car." You have one car. {kid} has been in a car you don't know about.

choices.label: "What did they look like?" (Stall.)

outcomes.text: "Crunchy." "What color?" "Crunchy." "A bag or a box?" "CRUNCHY." You open every cabinet. It's the rice cakes. It was always the rice cakes.

choices.label: Freeze

outcomes.text: Too slow. "YOU ATE THEM," {kid} announces, which, at some point in history, you did. The crunchy ones are gone. The debt is not.

title: Snack #3: The Audit
text: {kid} has emptied your bag onto the floor for a snack audit. Findings: four raisins from August, a cracker from a previous administration and one granola bar you said you didn't have.

choices.label: Surrender the bar. Cooperate fully.

outcomes.text: You hand it over. As a goodwill gesture, they return the August raisins to you. You eat them. It's the most fruit you've had since August.

choices.label: "That's my emergency bar."

outcomes.text: "Oh," they say gravely, and put it back in your bag. They pat the bag twice. You eat it later at a red light, in two bites, like a fugitive.
"Emergency," they repeat, thoughtfully. Then they lie down on the floor and have one. They're fast. They're very fast.

choices.label: Clean out the bag together. Make it a game.

outcomes.text: Trash, treasure or raisin. {kid} classifies a hair tie as a snack and a receipt as treasure. At the bottom: your spare car key, which you stopped looking for in June.

title: Diaper #1: Live Coverage
text: The bank. A silent line, nine people deep. {kid}, at full volume: "I'M POOPING." Nine heads turn. A pause. "STILL POOPING."

choices.label: "Thank you for the update."

outcomes.text: "Thank you for the update," you say, like a press secretary. "We'll have more at the top of the hour." The teller laughs. The man ahead laughs. "DONE POOPING," {kid} announces, and takes no questions.
"Thank you for the update." Nobody laughs. Someone in a blazer moves one place further away. "MORE POOPING," {kid} adds, as a correction.

choices.label: "Inside voice, please."

outcomes.text: "Inside voice," you whisper. {kid} nods and whispers, "I'm pooping," which is somehow worse, and carries further.
"Inside voice." They nod. Four minutes of perfect silence. Then, to the teller, at a normal volume: "I pooped. For you."

choices.label: Give up your place. Change them in the car.

outcomes.text: You change them on the back seat and come back to a line twelve deep. The teller waves you straight to the front: "For the updates."

title: Diaper #2: Standing Room Only
text: {kid} no longer lies down for diaper changes. Lying down is for babies. They will be changed standing up, walking away or, ideally, while running.

choices.label: Change them standing. Learn the footwork.

outcomes.text: You change a moving target on your knees in 41 seconds, using techniques you didn't know you had. {kid} never breaks stride. You're a professional now. There's no certificate.
Old one off. They're gone. A pantsless lap of the house follows, then a climb onto the couch, then a long look down at you from the top of it. Round two.

choices.label: Hand over your phone. Lie down for the screen.

outcomes.text: They lie down instantly, entranced. Change done in 20 seconds. Getting the phone back takes nine minutes and a negotiation over a video of a goose.
Perfectly still. Change done. When you get the phone back, there's a new alarm, labeled GOOSE, set for 4:10 AM. You can't find it to delete it. You'll both find it at 4:10.

choices.label: Let it ride. It's mostly pee.

outcomes.text: "Mostly" is doing a lot of work. An hour later it's doing all the work, and so is the couch cushion.

choices.label: Potty day 3. Skip the diaper. Shark underpants.

outcomes.text: They stand perfectly still for the shark underpants, which is all you've ever wanted. Two potty trips before lunch. You'd frame the underpants if that weren't strange.
They stand perfectly still for the shark underpants. Eleven minutes later, the shark is wet and so is the rug. "The shark did it."

title: Diaper #3: Size 2
text: Public bathroom. Diaper emergency. You dig through the bag. One diaper left: size 2, from a smaller, more innocent {kid}. They're a size 5.

choices.label: Make the size 2 work.

outcomes.text: It goes on like a swimsuit at a very expensive beach. It holds, technically, for nineteen minutes, which is all a diaper really owes you.
One tab reaches. The other tab is in a different time zone. You pull. It snaps, with a sound that echoes off the tile.

choices.label: Ask the parent at the sink. Beg if needed.

outcomes.text: The parent at the sink hands you a size 5 without a word and walks out, like a spy who was never there. You'll think of them on your deathbed.
"Oh, we're done with diapers," says the parent at the sink, and explains how it only took a weekend. You say "wow" four times and leave with nothing.

choices.label: Engineer one. Paper towels and a hair tie.

outcomes.text: You build a diaper from 14 paper towels and a hair tie. It holds all the way home. You could do this for a living. You'd earn more.
Fourteen paper towels and a hair tie. It holds until the parking lot, then turns back into paper towels, one at a time, in a trail behind you.

title: Diaper #4: The Pail
text: The diaper pail has been full for three days. You've been stomping it down with your foot. It makes a sound now when you open it. Not a smell. A sound.

choices.label: Empty it. Now. Hold your breath.

outcomes.text: You carry the bag out at arm's length, breathing through your mouth, then somehow through your ears. A neighbor watering their plants turns off the hose and goes inside.

choices.label: One more stomp.

outcomes.text: One more stomp. The lid closes. Then, slowly, on its own, it opens again, as if it has something to say.
The bag splits. You'll be cleaning the pail at 9 PM with a hose and the last of your will.

choices.label: Text {partner}: "whose turn is the pail"

outcomes.text: They do it tonight, gagging twice in the driveway, quietly, so the neighbors won't know. You watch from the window with deep, unspoken love.
You did. Days ago. Neither of you replies. The pail keeps the score.

chat.text: didn't you say you'd do it?

choices.label: Potty day 3. Throw out the pail. Burn the boats.

outcomes.text: Out goes the pail, and every diaper with it. Commitment works: three trips to the potty, the last one standing on the stool, announcing it to the street.
Out goes the pail and all hope of retreat. Forty minutes later there's an accident on the couch, and you're digging a diaper out of the outside bin.

title: Why? (63 So Far)
text: It's not even lunch and you've answered 63 whys. The chain began at "Why is it raining?" and has arrived, via clouds, Grandpa and the plumbing, at: "Why is there a hole in your hair?"

choices.label: "There isn't." Check the mirror.

outcomes.text: There is. A small, perfect clearing, right on top. {kid} spotted it from the couch. Why #64: "Can I touch it?"

choices.label: Answer honestly. Follicles. Genetics. Grandpa.

outcomes.text: You explain follicles, genetics and Grandpa. They listen to all of it. Why #64: "Why Grandpa?" You've been here all morning. You'll be here all afternoon.
You explain follicles and genetics. They nod slowly, then pat the hole in your hair, gently, as if it were a small pet. Why #64 never comes. You check the mirror anyway.

choices.label: "Because."

outcomes.text: "Because why?" Because because. "Because because why?" You've built a staircase with no top floor, and they're running up it.
"Oh," they say, satisfied. It worked. You'll never know why it worked. Now you have a why of your own.

title: Why? (Now 211)
text: Why #211 this week: "Why is the moon following the car?" You've started counting them in your phone, in the note where you used to write down ideas.

choices.label: "Because it loves you."

outcomes.text: "The moon loves me," they tell the window, then the moon, then a man at a gas station. You'll be hearing about it for years.
"Why?" "It just does." "Why does it just does?" The moon doesn't have to answer questions. You do.

choices.label: Pull over. Prove the moon isn't following.

outcomes.text: You pull into a parking lot to prove it. The car stops. The moon stops. "{ME}," {kid} whispers. "It's WAITING for us." You've proved the opposite, with science.

choices.label: Make something up. Confidently.

outcomes.text: "It's nosy." This is accepted at once. You've installed a nosy moon in their worldview. It will come up at every parent-teacher conference until fifth grade.
"It's lost," you say. {kid} gasps and spends the drive shouting directions out the window. "LEFT, MOON. LEFT." The moon misses the turn. So do you.

title: Why #1,000
text: Your phone note says 999. {kid} inhales. Why #1,000 of the week is coming, and you'd like it to be a good one. "Why do you write in your phone every time I say why?"

choices.label: Tell the truth: you're counting.

outcomes.text: "I'm counting your whys." A long pause. "Why?" That's 1,001.

choices.label: "It's a list of the best questions ever."

outcomes.text: They nod, proud, and spend the afternoon trying to get on the list. Why is the sky up. Why is shoes. Why is {partner}. The list grows by 140.

choices.label: "Why do YOU think?"

outcomes.text: They think about it. It's the first silence of the why phase. Then: "Because you love me." Then: "Why?" You'll take it.
They think. "Because you're old." They pat your hand. "And you forget." You write that down too.

choices.label: "The nosy moon tells me what to write."

outcomes.text: A gasp. The moon is nosy AND it texts you. The next note from daycare is a full page, double-sided.
